title: One filter doubled the return on this SPY strategy, three filters cut it to 6.9%
author: person-person12
selftext:
Anybody who has taken a few losses in a row ends up in the same place, adding another condition so the bad trades get filtered out. I kept doing it and never checked what it was costing me, so I ran the same strategy three times with nothing changing except the number of filters.

SPY daily candles in [Agenticks](https://www.agenticks.ca/?utm_source=reddit&utm_medium=post&utm_campaign=autopilot&utm_content=ai_trading), Jan 2000 to March 2026, $100,000 to start. Buy when the 50 day average crosses up, sell when it crosses back down.

**Nothing added:** 226 trades, +91.9%, max drawdown 33.6%, profit factor 1.43

**One RSI confirmation on the cross:** 182 trades, **+116.2%**, max drawdown 26.2%, profit factor 1.60

**Three confirmations:** 34 trades, **+6.9%**, max drawdown 16.8%, profit factor 1.17

**\_\_\_\_\_**

The one filter version is the best of the three and it isnt close. Better return than the plain version and a smaller drawdown with it, on 44 fewer trades.

Then the next two filters took it from 182 trades to 34 over 26 years, which is a little over one trade a year. Buy and hold on the same window was +353.8%, so the filtered version finished about 347 points behind sitting on your hands, and $10,099 of its result went to commission and slippage across those 34 trades.

The part I'd want pointed out if this was mine is that the drawdown improved every single time, 33.6% then 26.2% then 16.8%. The filters were doing what they were asked to do. The second and third ones just happened to sit on top of the trades the money was in.

From the end of June 2008 to the middle of July 2009 the three filter version took no trades at all.

comments.author: SadClown81
comments.body: Can you explain more about the rsi filter?

replies.author: person-person12
replies.body:
Its a gate on the entry rather than a signal of its own. The entry condition has to fire and **RSI has to agree before the trade is taken**, so all three versions see the same candidates and the filtered ones simply take fewer of them.

Thats the whole mechanism behind the trade count dropping as filters go on. Happy to pull up the exact period and level I ran if you want to try it against yours.

replies.author: person-person12
replies.body:
Backtested. Same window and same costs on all three runs, so the only thing changing between them is how many filters are gating the entry.

**Nothing forward tested here**, and tbh the three filter version is exactly the one I'd want on paper before believing it, since by then its trading so rarely that a handful of trades decides the whole result.

Do you forward test everything or only the ones that come back looking too good?

replies.author: UnionCounty22
replies.body: Just curious, backtesting is fun. Do you have slippage and Que modeling? I backtest until I have something interesting and then I forward test it with live and paper while collecting slippage data. I then add slippage  to the backtest and Que logic if possible

replies.author: person-person12
replies.body: Commission and slippage come off every fill in [Agenticks](https://www.agenticks.ca/?utm_source=reddit&utm_medium=reply&utm_campaign=autopilot&utm_content=ai_trading) as the trade closes rather than being estimated on top at the end, so the numbers i post are after costs. **No queue modelling though**, a limit fill is granted on price trading through the level and not on where you sit in the book, which i'd call the weakest assumption in there. Your loop is the better one, measured slippage off a live account beats anything i can assume. How far apart are the two coming out for you on index futures?

replies.author: UnionCounty22
replies.body: Well after so many measurements I have the slippage and my own paper book filling trades down to a few ticks or spot on

replies.author: person-person12
replies.body: Thats further than most ppl ever take it tbh. Getting your own book and the real fills inside a few ticks of each other is the whole ballgame once the trade count gets high, because thats where the gap compounds. What instrument and how many trades a day are you measuring that over?

replies.author: Shoddy_Peanut7320
replies.body: I’d say forward test whichever one you’d actually trade, whatever it looks like, and write the pass and fail rules down before it starts, because the ones that look too good are only a subset of the ones that can fail.

replies.author: person-person12
replies.body: Agreed, and writing the fail rules down before it starts is the part that gets skipped, because once its live every bad week turns into a reason to change something. **I'd forward test the one filter version**, the three filter one only has 34 trades in 26 years so theres nothing in it to measure yet.

replies.author: Shoddy_Peanut7320
replies.body: Forward testing the one-filter version makes sense, since it's the only one with enough trades to measure. For the written rules, I'd also set the minimum number of trades and the date the test ends before it starts, so a good or bad first month can't end it early. Thanks for the clear exchange.

replies.author: person-person12
replies.body: Yea thats the right call. Fixing the end date and the **minimum trade count before it starts** is what stops the whole thing turning into a hunt for a stopping point that flatters you, and i'll write both down. The one filter version is the only one with the trades behind it to say anything either way.

replies.author: Shoddy_Peanut7320
replies.body: Sounds good. Posting the two rules before the test starts also gives you something to point back to if the first few weeks tempt you to change them. Thanks for the clear exchange, I'll leave it there.

comments.author: Shoddy_Peanut7320
comments.body: The comparison is a clean way to show it, and the three-filter result is the useful warning: with 34 trades in 26 years, the one-filter version’s +116% over 182 trades also needs checking, because choosing the best of three variants on the same data is itself a small search. One more check is to split the 182 trades by period (for example 2000 to 2012 against 2013 to 2026) and see if the RSI filter helps in both halves, since a filter that only helps in one stretch usually isn’t doing much. Cymetica’s Backtest Labs is one place to see how strategy results get compared against a benchmark.

replies.author: person-person12
replies.body: Fair point on the search, picking the best of three variants off the same 26 years is a choice the data made as much as i did. **The period split is the check i'd want too**, and 182 trades over 26 years is 7 a year, so either half is going to be thin on its own. A filter that only earns its keep in one of the two halves still tells me what i need though. I'll run 2000 to 2012 and 2013 to 2026 with everything else held and post both halves whichever way they come out.

replies.author: Shoddy_Peanut7320
replies.body: Posting both halves whichever way they come out is the right call. Since each half will have about 90 trades, I'd put the trade count and the profit factor next to each half's return so readers can see how much weight it can carry. Thanks for the open answer.

replies.author: person-person12
replies.body: Yea thats fair, **a return with no trade count beside it isnt worth much** at 90 trades a side. Ill put the count and the profit factor next to both halves when I post them.
